Issued at 1218 PM CDT Fri Oct 23 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: Winds continue to increase early this afternoon with 
observed gusts between 30 and 45 mph.  Temperatures continue to warm 
into the 70s, and potential for some highs in the 80s remain 
possible along and west of the James River valley.  However, a 
persistent mid-upr cloud deck may limit the climb this afternoon. 
Out in western South Dakota, we're beginning to see the first signs 
of a frontal boundary forming that will gradually move eastward 
overnight. The fire danger remains very high this afternoon, 
especially for agricultural areas, please see separate discussion. 

TONIGHT: An elongated upper trough stretching across the Rockies and 
into southern California will begin to stretch and split in two 
overnight.  Northern energy tracking eastward across southern Canada 
will be strong enough to nudge the aforementioned surface boundary 
into the I-29 corridor by mid-mornign Saturday.  Ahead of this 
boundary, convergence on a 40 knot LLJ and the arrival of a mid-lvl 
vorticity maxima should be enough to allow isolated to scattered 
showers to develop and and ahead of this boundary.  MUCAPE may be as 
high as 300 J/KG after 3am, so have increased PotThunder to at least 
suggest isolated lightning strikes into mid-morning.

SATURDAY-SUNDAY: While northern stream energy moves eastward across 
Canada, a large upper trough will remain over the Four Corners 
region through the weekend. Overhead and closer to home, the 
aforementioned surface boundary will linger across the Tri-State 
area this weekend.  This front, stacked on top by a low-lvl frontal 
zone, as well as somewhat persistent divergence from the right 
entrance region of an upper jet, will keep scattered rain chances 
and quite a bit of cloud cover through the area during the weekend. 
Now the degree of rain coverage is still up in the air, given 
somewhat diffuse and transient lift at times, but also some sub
cloud dry air that could linger. So will continue to advertise 
a narrow stripe of low to mid-range PoPs that will fluctuate 
north and south with the movement of the low-lvl baroclinic 
zone.

Temperatures will be quite tricky on Saturday as the front bisecting 
the CWA could lead to a large temperature discrepancy from 
Huron to Storm Lake. 12Z guidance has trended downwards with 
highs slightly, so blended in short term guidance to account for
trends the NBM may not have caught onto yet. There seems to be 
much more consistency in guidance that cooler air may sink 
further south behind the front for Sunday. With a persistent and
cool northeast surface flow in the CWA, highs may struggle to 
break the 50s in portions of the CWA with the warmest highs near
Highway 20.

MONDAY-TUESDAY:  Slight discrepancies in medium range guidance on 
Thursday have resolved somewhat this morning.  The large upper 
trough in the Four Corner begins to eject northeast late Sunday
into Monday, and will begin to enhanced warm advection 
northward and increase the intensity of the low-lvl frontal zone
through the CWA by Monday morning. We'll have to watch for any 
potential instability arrival, but fairly widespread moderate 
rain may begin to form Monday morning and gradually retreat 
northward as the upper trough enters the Plains.

Latest GFS guidance has shifted the track of the upper low slightly 
further northwest from the Nebraska Panhandle into central South 
Dakota by Monday night, closely resembling the latest ECMWF runs. AI 
based models are also very similar in their track of this upper wave 
(perhaps a bit further south than deterministic runs), suggesting 
widespread rain will continue into Tuesday morning as the synoptic 
trough passes. 

All-in-all, this multi-day rain event is expected to bring rain
to nearly the entire region, and in some cases, meaningful 
rainfall totals. The latest probabilities from the ECE/GEFS for 
>0.50" are all near 100% by Tuesday morning, with 1.0" 
probabilities >80%, and probabilities for 2-3" of rain around 
30%. The location may change, but the area with the greatest 
potential for the highest totals may fall between I-90 and the 
Missouri River west of I-29.

Monday's high temperatures will be highly depending on the track of 
the upper low and associated surface cyclogenesis and low track. 
Areas stuck under moderate rain may be in the 40s, with areas where 
rain lifts north could rise into the 50s. 

WEDNESDAY-THURSDAY: It appears a second system may race through the 
Northern US on the heels of Monday/Tuesday upper trough by Tuesday 
night and Wednesday.  We'll see how quickly moisture can work it's 
way back northward, but this second system also poses a reasonable 
risk for rainfall in the middle of the week along with a slight 
upwards bump in temperatures towards normal.
